newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan admits budget in trouble.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan admits budget in trouble.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan admitted on Tuesday for the first time that his government's 1997 budget was in trouble.

"The budget was balanced in the first and second months. I am following it closely and in the third month big difficulties began to emerge," he told his party meeting in parliament, confirming the fears of many economic analysts.

The coalition government has programmed a zero deficit for 1997 after a deficit of 1,217 trillion lira ($9 billion) in 1996. Erbakan had said earlier the budget produced surplus in the first two months of this year.
But economists said the surplus was only a result of accounting tricks, estimating the total first quarter deficit at over 300 trillion lira ($2.2 billion).
The finance ministry, which disclosed budgetary aggregates for each month previous to 1997, has yet to unveil any budget results so far this year.
Erbakan said the government still aimed for a zero deficit this year, despite current problems which he said were caused by an "artifical crisis" created by the opposition and Turkish press.

But analysts say the budget target is not realistic in view of slow privatisations and such "black holes" as the poor social security system and costly public enterprises draining large sums from budgetary funds.

Erbakan's remarks came shortly after he told the same meeting that his Welfare Party, senior member of the coalition with conservatives led by his deputy Tansu Ciller, was ready for elections "at any moment."

Facing mounting challenges to his authority from the army and others in the secularist establishment, Erbakan also said earlier in the day that there was no credible alternative to his coalition government.
He blamed press reports criticising his government for creating "artificial agendas that have disrupted economic stability" in the country.

Political uncertainty sent stocks down about five percent over the last week by Monday's close, while money market rates rose to an average 90 percent from 80 percent over the same period. Financial markets were relatively steady on Tuesday.
Economists blame big budget deficits, at over eight percent of the gross national product last year, for inflation running at around 80 percent a year.
Erbakan said the government had successfully kept Turkey away from foreign borrowing, unpopular at home.
"Turkey has not been receiving any foreign debt for 10 months," he said.
However, Turkey issued two sets of Eurobonds -- a 500-million mark and a 300-Italian lire -- in the first quarter of this year.
Officials say a plan for a third Euro issue of $250 million, has been delayed over high volatility in the U.S. treasuries market.
Economists say Turkey must borrow in international markets to service its foreign debt obligations -- around $8 billion a year -- on time. ($1=135,300 lira)
